chapter_title: Protecting Data at Rest and in Transit

screens.title: Protecting Data at Rest and in Transit
screens.subtitle: TDE, Always Encrypted, SSL/TLS, and key management for Azure databases

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn how Azure protects data both where it lives and as it moves. We will clarify two complementary approaches: disk-level protection with Transparent Data Encryption, and client-side column protection with Always Encrypted, plus the network protections provided by SSL and TLS. You will see why TDE is a broad safety net for storage and backups, and why Always Encrypted is used when DBAs must not be able to view sensitive column values. We will also cover keys: the difference between keys managed by the service and keys you manage in Azure Key Vault, and why that separation supports compliance and key rotation. Throughout, I’ll point out common mistakes — for example, relying only on server defaults without requiring encryption on the client — and practical verification steps you can run with SSMS or CLI. By the end of this chapter you’ll know which features to apply for confidentiality versus storage protection, how client drivers participate in Always Encrypted, and what to check to prove your data is protected. Consider a scenario where credit card numbers must never be visible to DBAs but must be searchable; we’ll use that to guide choices.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Use TDE to encrypt stored files and backups, Always Encrypted to keep column values hidden from DBAs, and SSL/TLS to protect data in transit. Use Key Vault and CMKs when you need control over key lifecycle and audits.

narration.text: These objectives describe the practical skills you will develop in this chapter. First, you will implement Transparent Data Encryption for Azure S Q L Database, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, and MySQL so that your database files, logs, and backups are encrypted at rest. You will learn the concrete commands and portal steps to verify the encryption state. Second, you will differentiate service-managed keys from customer-managed keys and learn how to integrate CMK with Azure Key Vault. That includes why separation of duties and key rotation matter. Third, you will configure Always Encrypted for sensitive columns so that clients encrypt data before it reaches the database engine; you will see how CEKs and CMKs work together and how client drivers participate. Finally, you will ensure data in transit is encrypted by enforcing SSL/TLS on client connections and learn what parameters to add to connection strings. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you can prove competency in a lab or production environment.

keyIdea.title: Objective summary
keyIdea.text: By combining TDE, Always Encrypted, CMK in Key Vault, and strict TLS settings you create layered protection for stored and moving data.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical verification
screens.subtitle: How you'll prove each skill in the lab

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on how you will prove competence. You will verify TDE state using system DM queries in SSMS or CLI, and observe encryption_state values that indicate active encryption. You will configure CMK with Azure Key Vault, then grant the database server access and confirm Key Vault integrations. For Always Encrypted, you will use the SSMS Encrypt Columns wizard to create a Column Master Key and Column Encryption Key with Azure Key Vault as the CMK source, then test querying from a client with and without client-side decryption enabled to observe the encrypted binary values. For TLS, you will update connection strings to include explicit parameters such as Encrypt=True for S Q L Server and Ssl Mode=Require for PostgreSQL, and then confirm the session is encrypted. Each verification step shows you what to run and what output proves the control is working, so you can demonstrate security and compliance during operations or audits.

screens.title: Understanding data at rest vs data in transit
screens.subtitle: Why you need distinct protections for stored files and network traffic

narration.text: When we speak of protecting data at rest versus data in transit, we are separating two different attack surfaces. Data at rest refers to data stored on disk, in backups, and in log files. The principal risk is unauthorized access to storage media or snapshots. Transparent Data Encryption addresses this surface by encrypting files and logs at the storage layer so stolen disks or backups do not reveal plaintext. Data in transit is the data that travels across networks between clients and the database. The main risk here is interception or man‑in‑the‑middle attacks. SSL and TLS protect the wire, ensuring confidentiality and integrity while messages travel. A common misconception is that encrypting storage alone is enough; it is not. Without TLS, credentials or queries can be observed in transit. Another mistake is assuming TLS defaults on the client side are sufficient; you must require encryption in the client connection string to prevent downgrade attacks. For example, S Q L Server clients should include Encrypt=True and TrustServerCertificate=False to enforce TLS. In practice you will use layered controls: TDE to protect stored files, Always Encrypted to protect sensitive columns even from privileged users, and TLS to secure the network. Which control you choose depends on the threat: unauthorized physical access points to TDE, while privileged database users point to Always Encrypted.

keyIdea.title: Distinguish surfaces
keyIdea.text: Use storage encryption for disk-level threats, TLS for network threats, and client-side encryption when insiders must be prevented from seeing values.

content.html:
Core Concept › At rest vs In transit
Data at rest
Files, transaction logs, and backups stored on disk or cloud storage.
Transparent Data Encryption (TDE)
Performs real-time I/O encryption and decryption at the storage layer. Transparent to applications.
Concrete example
If a backup file is copied from storage, TDE ensures the file remains encrypted and unreadable without the keys.
Key Takeaway

TDE protects storage-level artifacts but does not limit what privileged DB engine users can see when data is decrypted in memory.

Data in transit
Client-server network traffic between applications and the database.
SSL / TLS
Provides encryption and integrity for network sessions; prevent eavesdropping and tampering.
Concrete example
Adding Encrypt=True to a SQL Server connection string forces the client to negotiate TLS with the server, protecting credentials and queries in transit.
Common mistake

Relying on server defaults without requiring encryption in the client can leave connections vulnerable to downgrade attacks.

screens.title: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE)
screens.subtitle: What TDE protects and how it works in Azure

narration.text: Transparent Data Encryption encrypts the storage artifacts of a database — the data files, the transaction logs, and backups — by performing real‑time encryption and decryption as data is written and read from disk. The word transparent reflects that applications do not need code changes: the database engine handles encryption at the input and output layer. In Azure S Q L Database, TDE is enabled by default for new databases; for Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL you can enable it via portal or CLI. TDE helps mitigate threats like theft of backups or unauthorized access to raw storage. However, it does not protect data from users who can query decrypted data through the engine, such as a privileged DBA. That limitation is important: if your requirement is to prevent DBAs from seeing sensitive column values, you need Always Encrypted. Another key operational idea is key management: TDE uses encryption keys that can be service-managed by Microsoft or customer-managed in Azure Key Vault. Choosing CMK gives you control over rotation and revocation and allows separate responsibilities between DB admins and security admins. A practical verification step is to query the system view that reports encryption_state; an active state confirms TDE is in effect.

keyIdea.title: TDE insight
keyIdea.text: TDE secures stored files and backups without changing applications, but it does not hide plaintext from the database engine or authorized queries.

content.html:
Definition › Transparent Data Encryption
How TDE works
TDE performs real-time I/O encryption and decryption at the storage layer; reads bring decrypted data into memory, writes persist encrypted bytes to disk.
Scope
Encrypts database files, transaction logs, and backups.
Operational note
Transparent to applications; enable via portal or CLI for supported services.
Key Takeaway

TDE protects stored artifacts from offline exposure but not against in‑engine access by DBAs.

Enablement and verification
Enable TDE via the Azure portal or CLI, then verify encryption status using the system DM view.
Verification query
SELECT DB_NAME(database_id) AS DatabaseName, encryption_state, percent_complete, key_algorithm, key_length
FROM sys.dm_database_encryption_keys;
Note: encryption_state = 3 indicates the database is encrypted.
CLI example
az postgres flexible-server parameter set \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --server-name MyPostgresServer \
  --name azure.enable_data_encryption_at_rest \
  --value ON

screens.title: Service-managed keys vs Customer-managed keys (CMK)
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs: simplicity versus control and auditability

narration.text: TDE keys can be managed by Microsoft as a service-managed option or by you as a customer-managed key stored in Azure Key Vault. Service-managed keys are convenient: the service takes care of key lifecycle and rotation and reduces operational overhead. That simplicity is useful for many applications, but it reduces direct control over when keys are rotated or revoked. Customer-managed keys are stored in Azure Key Vault and give you control over the key lifecycle, including rotation schedules and revocation. CMK supports stronger compliance needs because security teams can audit key access and integrate policies. A common implementation pattern is to use CMK for databases that hold regulated or highly confidential data while using service-managed keys for less-sensitive workloads. Integrating CMK requires additional steps: create a Key Vault key, grant the database server access, and configure the server to use the Key Vault key. A misconception is that CMK is inherently more secure; CMK gives you control, but it also increases responsibility: you must manage rotation and ensure availability to the database to avoid interruptions. Always document access policies and test key rotation to ensure your database can still decrypt data after rotation.

keyIdea.title: Key management trade-off
keyIdea.text: Service-managed keys reduce operational work; CMK in Key Vault gives control and auditability but requires lifecycle management and testing.

content.html:
Comparison › Service-managed vs Customer-managed Keys
Service-managed keys
Microsoft manages key creation, rotation, and storage. Minimal configuration and low operational burden.
  • Pros: simplicity, less administration, automatic rotation.
  • Cons: limited control over key lifecycle and audit events.
When to use
Non-regulated workloads or where operational simplicity is a priority.
Customer-managed keys (CMK)
Keys live in Azure Key Vault under your control. You manage rotation, revocation, and access policies for compliance and audits.
  • Pros: full control, auditable access, integration with security processes.
  • Cons: increased responsibility to rotate and maintain key availability.
Implementation notes
Create a Key Vault key, grant the DB server access, then configure TDE to use that key. Test rotation to avoid service disruption.

screens.title: Integrating CMK with Azure Key Vault
screens.subtitle: Steps to provision a key and grant database access

narration.text: Integrating customer-managed keys requires a clear sequence of tasks. First create or import a key into Azure Key Vault. Next, grant the database server a managed identity or service principal permission to unwrap and use the key. Then configure the database to reference the Key Vault key as the TDE protector. For Always Encrypted you also create a Column Master Key stored in Key Vault and a Column Encryption Key that uses that master key. The separation of duties matters: security administrators manage keys, while DBAs manage the database. This separation enables rotation and revocation without giving DBAs direct key control. A common pitfall is forgetting to grant the server principal the right Key Vault access policies; without those permissions the database cannot use the CMK and encryption operations will fail. Another operational detail is to test key rotation: rotate a key in Key Vault and confirm the database can still decrypt existing data or that rewrapping steps succeed. Practically, after granting access you configure the server to use the Key Vault key and then verify the configuration in the portal or with the appropriate CLI commands. This process gives you audit logs and lifecycle control over encryption keys.

keyIdea.title: CMK integration
keyIdea.text: Provision a Key Vault key, grant database access, configure the server to use the key, and test rotation and access to ensure continuity.

content.html:
Process Flow › Key Vault Integration
Step-by-step
  1. Create or import a key in Azure Key Vault and note its identifier.
  2. Grant the database server's managed identity or service principal permission to use the key (unwrap/wrap).
  3. Configure the database server to use the Key Vault key as the TDE protector or as the Column Master Key for Always Encrypted.
  4. Verify by checking the portal or running verification queries; then test key rotation scenarios.
Operational caution
Ensure Key Vault is reachable and that access policies allow the database to use the key. A missing permission is a common cause of failure.
Example annotation
Role separation: Security Team creates and rotates keys in Key Vault; DB Team configures databases to reference those keys but does not hold key material.
Check your understanding
What happens if you rotate a key and the database lacks access to the new key? You may lose the ability to decrypt until access is restored or rewrapping is completed.

screens.title: Always Encrypted: Client-side column protection
screens.subtitle: How Always Encrypted keeps values hidden from the database engine

narration.text: Always Encrypted moves encryption and decryption to the client driver so that sensitive column values are encrypted before they ever reach the database engine. The database stores only ciphertext and never has access to the column master keys used to unwrap the data. This is particularly useful when compliance or policy requires that database administrators cannot view plaintext values. Implementing Always Encrypted requires two key objects: a Column Master Key, typically stored in Azure Key Vault, and a Column Encryption Key, which is used to encrypt actual column values. Client drivers such as ADO. NET or JDBC must be configured with access to the Column Master Key so that they can perform encryption and decryption on the client side. A practical example is encrypting a credit card column: the client encrypts the credit card value before insertion; a DBA querying the database without client-side decryption sees only binary ciphertext. A common misconception is that Always Encrypted supports all S Q L operations; it supports limited operations like equality comparisons with deterministic encryption but does not support pattern searches or many computations on encrypted data. Choose encryption type—deterministic or randomized—based on whether you need equality searches.

keyIdea.title: Always Encrypted insight
keyIdea.text: Always Encrypted protects column values from DBAs by performing encryption in client drivers and storing only ciphertext in the database.

content.html:
Definition › Always Encrypted
Core idea
Clients encrypt and decrypt sensitive column values so the database engine never sees the plaintext.
Components
Column Master Key (CMK) in Key Vault and Column Encryption Key (CEK) used by the client driver.
Concrete example
A client application encrypts a credit card number before INSERT; without client-side decryption, SSMS shows ciphertext for that column.
Limitations

Operations on encrypted columns are limited. Use deterministic encryption for equality searches and randomized for stronger confidentiality without searchability.

Developer note
Client drivers must be configured with access to the CMK for transparent encryption and decryption in applications.
C# snippet (visual)
string connectionString = "Data Source=myserver.database.windows.net;Initial Catalog=mydatabase;Column Encryption Setting=Enabled;";
using (SqlConnection connection = new SqlConnection(connectionString))
{
  connection.Open();
  using (SqlCommand command = new SqlCommand("INSERT INTO Customers (SSN, Name) VALUES (@ssn, @name);", connection))
  {
    command.Parameters.AddWithValue("@ssn", "123-45-678");
    command.Parameters.AddWithValue("@name", "John Doe");
    command.ExecuteNonQuery();
  }
}

screens.title: Implementing Always Encrypted with SSMS
screens.subtitle: Wizard steps and what you should verify

narration.text: The SSMS Encrypt Columns wizard guides you through implementing Always Encrypted and creating the required keys. Start by selecting Tasks → Encrypt Columns on the database. Choose the column to encrypt, for example CreditCardNumber, and pick the encryption type: deterministic for equality searches or randomized for stronger protection without searchability. Next create a new Column Encryption Key and a Column Master Key; for CMK choose Azure Key Vault as the source and sign in to select your Key Vault. The wizard will offer to proceed immediately or generate a PowerShell script for automation. If you proceed, it will create the CMK and CEK and rewrite the column data to ciphertext. Verification is essential: after the wizard completes, connect without client-side decryption and run a SELECT to observe ciphertext for the encrypted column. Then connect with a client configured for Always Encrypted to confirm you can see plaintext. A common mistake is not ensuring the client has access to the CMK in Key Vault; without that, client decryption will fail. Another pitfall is choosing randomized encryption when your application requires equality lookups. Test the chosen encryption type for your query patterns before finalizing.

keyIdea.title: Wizard checklist
keyIdea.text: Use the SSMS wizard to create CMK and CEK, choose deterministic or randomized encryption, and verify behavior both with and without client-side decryption.

content.html:
Process Flow › Always Encrypted Wizard
Wizard steps
  1. Right-click database → Tasks → Encrypt Columns to launch the wizard.
  2. Select the target column (e.g., CreditCardNumber) and choose encryption type.
  3. Create a new Column Encryption Key and a Column Master Key; choose Azure Key Vault as CMK source.
  4. Run the operation or generate an automation script; then verify results in SSMS and from clients.
Verification steps
After encryption, connect without client-side decryption and run a SELECT to see ciphertext. Then connect with an application configured for Always Encrypted and confirm plaintext is available to the application only.
Example choices
Choose deterministic encryption if you require equality joins or lookups. Choose randomized if you prioritize stronger confidentiality and do not need equality comparisons.
Common pitfall
Selecting randomized encryption while the application needs equality searches will break lookups. Test encryption types with your queries first.

screens.title: Verifying TDE status and common checks
screens.subtitle: Queries and CLI commands you should know

narration.text: Verification is straightforward and essential. To confirm TDE state on S Q L Server or Azure S Q L, run the dynamic management view query that lists encryption details. The query returns the database name, encryption state, percent complete, and key algorithm. An encryption_state value of three indicates the database is encrypted. For Azure Database for PostgreSQL, enabling data encryption at rest can be done through the Azure CLI parameter; an example command sets the parameter azure. enable_data_encryption_at_rest to ON. Always inspect the server’s Key Vault integration and permissions after enabling CMK. A practical verification sequence is: run the DM view, check the portal TDE configuration, and validate Key Vault access logs for key unwrap events. Another common check is to connect both with and without client-side encryption when testing Always Encrypted to observe ciphertext. Mistakes to avoid include assuming TDE implies DBAs cannot view plaintext and forgetting to require TLS on the client. These simple checks let you produce evidence during audits and ensure your encryption settings are active and functioning. Verifying TDE status and common checks means use the dm view for tde status, azure cli to enable storage encryption, and test client behavior to demonstrate always encrypted effectiveness.. In practical terms, queries and cli commands you should know. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Verification commands
keyIdea.text: Use the dm view for TDE status, Azure CLI to enable storage encryption, and test client behavior to demonstrate Always Encrypted effectiveness.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › Verification Queries
TDE verification (SQL)
SELECT DB_NAME(database_id) AS DatabaseName, encryption_state, percent_complete, key_algorithm, key_length
FROM sys.dm_database_encryption_keys;
Note: encryption_state = 3 indicates the database is encrypted.
CLI example (PostgreSQL)
az postgres flexible-server parameter set \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --server-name MyPostgresServer \
  --name azure.enable_data_encryption_at_rest \
  --value ON
Always Encrypted verification
Connect without client-side encryption and run a SELECT to see ciphertext; then connect with an application configured for Always Encrypted to view decrypted values. This proves client-side keys are required for plaintext access.
Operational checklist
  • Confirm Key Vault access policies and audit logs.
  • Test key rotation to ensure database continuity.
  • Enforce TLS on all clients to secure transit.

screens.title: Enforcing SSL/TLS for client connections
screens.subtitle: Connection string parameters and common client-side mistakes

narration.text: Ensuring data in transit is encrypted requires more than relying on server defaults. Clients must be configured to require TLS. For S Q L Server clients, include Encrypt=True and TrustServerCertificate=False in the connection string so the client insists on a valid server certificate and refuses unencrypted sessions. For PostgreSQL, include Ssl Mode=Require to force SSL/TLS. If the client is left to accept encryption optionally, an attacker may attempt a downgrade to an unencrypted connection. Another common oversight is trusting the server certificate without validation, which allows man‑in‑the‑middle risks if certificates are not validated. In Azure the services generally enforce TLS by default, but you must still update your application connection strings and SDKs to require it explicitly. A practical check is to inspect your client connection strings across environments and ensure the required parameters are present. For languages and drivers, consult the driver documentation for the appropriate parameter names and verify that TLS negotiation succeeds; if not, check firewall and network rules that might block the secure handshake. Requiring TLS on the client side is a small change with large security impact.

keyIdea.title: Enforce on clients
keyIdea.text: Always require TLS in client connection strings and validate server certificates to prevent downgrades and man-in-the-middle attacks.

content.html:
Definition › SSL/TLS Enforcement
SQL Server example
Server=tcp:myserver.database.windows.net,1433;Initial Catalog=mydatabase;Persist Security Info=False;User ID={your_username};Password={your_password};Encrypt=True;TrustServerCertificate=False;Connection Timeout=30;
Encrypt=True forces TLS; TrustServerCertificate=False ensures proper certificate validation.
PostgreSQL example
Host=mypgserver.postgres.database.azure.com;Port=5432;Database=mydatabase;Username=myuser;Password=mypassword;Ssl Mode=Require;
Ssl Mode=Require ensures the client negotiates an encrypted session.
Common mistakes
  • Not including encryption parameters in the client connection string.
  • Setting TrustServerCertificate=True in production, which bypasses certificate validation.
  • Assuming server defaults guarantee client enforcement of TLS.

screens.title: Deterministic vs Randomized encryption in Always Encrypted
screens.subtitle: Choosing encryption types based on query and privacy needs

narration.text: Always Encrypted offers two main encryption types for columns: deterministic and randomized. Deterministic encryption produces the same ciphertext for the same plaintext when encrypted under the same key, which enables equality comparisons, joins, and point lookups on encrypted columns. Randomized encryption adds random noise so the same plaintext encrypts to different ciphertexts each time, providing stronger confidentiality but preventing equality searches. Choose deterministic when your application must perform exact-match lookups, for example locating a customer record by credit card number. Choose randomized when you want maximum confidentiality and can avoid equality searches. A typical misconception is to assume deterministic is insecure; deterministic is less private but necessary for some queries, while randomized is stronger but limits functionality. Always evaluate query patterns: if equality searches are frequent, deterministic may be necessary, but you should apply it only to the minimal set of columns and pair it with other protections such as TDE and CMK. Test your queries after choosing an encryption type to ensure performance and functionality meet requirements. Deterministic vs Randomized encryption in Always Encrypted means use deterministic for equality searches and randomized for stronger confidentiality; apply the least permissive choice that supports required queries.. In practical terms, choosing encryption types based on query and privacy needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Encryption type choice
keyIdea.text: Use deterministic for equality searches and randomized for stronger confidentiality; apply the least permissive choice that supports required queries.

content.html:
Comparison › Deterministic vs Randomized
Deterministic
Same plaintext yields same ciphertext, enabling equality comparisons and lookups.
  • Use when application needs exact-match searches.
  • Weaker confidentiality compared to randomized.
Randomized
Stronger confidentiality; same plaintext encrypts differently each time, preventing equality searches.
  • Use when searchability is not required.
  • Preferred for highly sensitive columns where lookups are not needed.
Decision tip

Apply the least permissive encryption type that still supports your application queries and verify performance and correctness after encryption.

screens.title: Data classification and operational practices
screens.subtitle: How classification informs encryption choices and maintenance tasks

narration.text: Data classification is the process of labeling data according to sensitivity, value, and regulatory requirements. Typical labels are Public, Confidential, and Highly Confidential. Classification helps prioritize which columns and datasets require protections such as Always Encrypted or CMK-backed TDE. Start by discovering sensitive data with tools and then assign labels that map to controls: highly confidential data often needs Always Encrypted and CMK, confidential data may require TDE with CMK, while public data may not need encryption beyond TLS in transit. Operational practices include regular verification of encryption states, auditing key usage in Key Vault, rotating keys according to policy, and testing rotations in non-production first. Common mistakes include failing to classify data before applying encryption, which can lead to unnecessary complexity, and not automating rotation and verification, which risks expired or inaccessible keys. Finally, document your classification-to-control mapping so auditors and operators understand why each control was applied. A practical practice: inventory columns with personal data, decide which must be hidden from DBAs, and then apply Always Encrypted selectively to those columns while using TDE broadly for storage protections.

keyIdea.title: Classification drives controls
keyIdea.text: Label data by sensitivity, then apply Always Encrypted for highly confidential columns and TDE/CMK for storage-level protections; automate rotation and verification.

content.html:
Process › Classification & Ops
Classification workflow
  1. Discover sensitive columns and assign sensitivity labels (Public, Confidential, Highly Confidential).
  2. Map labels to controls: Always Encrypted for highest sensitivity, TDE with CMK for storage-level protection, TLS for transit.
  3. Implement controls selectively to minimize disruption and maximize privacy.
  4. Automate key rotation and verification; keep audit trails for compliance.
Operational tips
  • Test key rotation in staging before production.
  • Document why each column was encrypted and who controls the keys.
  • Monitor Key Vault audit logs for unexpected access patterns.
Why it matters

Classification ensures you spend effort protecting the most sensitive data and maintain a defensible security posture during audits.

narration.text: Let's reinforce the most important concepts. Transparent Data Encryption secures database files, logs, and backups at the storage layer so stolen media remains unreadable. Always Encrypted moves encryption to the client so sensitive column values remain ciphertext inside the database engine, protecting them even from privileged DBAs. SSL and TLS protect data in transit by encrypting the network channel so credentials and queries cannot be eavesdropped. Each concept protects a different surface, and the right combination depends on your threat model and compliance requirements. As you design controls, keep in mind that TDE protects offline artifacts, Always Encrypted protects against insider access to column values, and TLS protects the wire. Ask yourself: given my data classification labels, which surfaces must I defend to meet policy and regulatory needs? keyIdea.text: TDE, Always Encrypted, and TLS form a layered defense: storage, client, and network protections respectively.

content.html:
What to Remember › Key Concepts
Transparent Data Encryption
Encrypts database files, logs, and backups at the storage layer.
Always Encrypted
Client-side column encryption that keeps values hidden from the engine.
SSL / TLS
Encrypts network traffic between clients and database servers to prevent eavesdropping.
Summary takeaway
Combine these protections according to your data classification and compliance requirements to cover storage, client, and network threats.

narration.text: A few more short concepts to remember. Customer-managed keys let you control key lifecycle in Azure Key Vault; they enable rotation, revocation, and audit trails. Azure Key Vault is the secure store for keys and is central to implementing CMK for TDE and as a Column Master Key for Always Encrypted. Data classification assigns sensitivity labels so you can decide which controls to apply; it prevents over-encryption and helps focus resources on the most important data. Together these pieces support a defensible security posture: Key Vault and CMK provide custody and auditability while classification ensures you protect the right data with the right controls. As a practice, document mappings between labels and protections and periodically test both key rotations and client-side decryptions to ensure resilience. content.html:
What to Remember › Vault & Classification
Customer-managed Keys (CMK)
Keys you control in Key Vault for rotation and audit.
Azure Key Vault
Securely stores keys and provides audit logs for key usage.
Data Classification
Label data to map sensitivity to controls and to prioritize protections.
Final takeaway
Combine classification, Key Vault custody, and the appropriate encryption features to create a layered, auditable protection strategy.
